concept.name: Negative convexity
concept.definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is concave: prices rise less when yields fall and fall more when yields rise than duration alone predicts. It is typical of callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities, whose cash flows shorten when rates decline (calls/prepayments) and lengthen when rates rise.
concept.intuition: The bond works against you both ways: it stops appreciating just when rates fall (because it gets called or prepaid) and keeps falling when rates rise.
concept.mechanics: Convexity is the second derivative of price with respect to yield, approximated as (P(−) + P(+) − 2P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); when this quantity is negative, duration rises as yields rise (extension risk) and falls as yields fall (contraction risk), making duration-only hedges systematically wrong in the adverse direction.
concept.formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); negative when P(−) + P(+) < 2 × P_0.
concept.failure_modes: Duration-based estimates fail precisely when they are most needed (large rate moves) for negatively convex securities; hedging MBS or callable books with duration alone creates pro-cyclical hedging flows that can amplify rate swings.
concept.misconceptions: Negative convexity does not mean the bond must lose money; it means the price response is asymmetric, and investors are compensated for bearing it through higher yield (option-adjusted spread).
concept.example: A callable bond priced at 100 might gain only 3 points if yields fall 100 bp (its price is capped near the call price) but lose 6 points if yields rise 100 bp.
